It's an interesting concept, but it has some significant issues working against it.

Plastics (especially PET from things like bottles) will wear at a higher rate than the crushed stone used in asphalt roads (asphalt is a combination of bitumen and gravel or sand). Most plastics are susceptible to UV damage at a much higher rate than stone, in addition to being effected to a higher degree by chemicals (think things like oil, grease, automotive fluids, de-icing solutions, etc).

Asphalt roads are pretty easy (and cheap) to maintain and it's a fantastically "green" product. Over 99% of all the asphalt in the US is recycled into new asphalt. There is equipment that will do "in line" resurfacing already out there (i.e. it chews up old at the front of the machine, remelts in the middle, and lays down new at the back of the machine). Asphalt roads are readily patched in the event repair work or under-road construction needs to happen (water main breaks, pipe repairs, etc) and virtually ever road and street department in the country already has the equipment to do this kind of work. It wears well, handles temperature extremes without much issue, has great traction properties and is flexible enough to conform to geography.

So while I think it's a neat idea, the existing materials the "Lego Road" is up against are far better suited to the job, at least as of right now. That some street departments are to broke to afford to maintain their roads is a whole other issue, one that won't be solved by a new road surface material.

Sure, I mean, the density of asphalt roads is already higher than most plastic materials to begin with, especially when compacted with a steam roller. Even then you see compression wear from the tires forming "grooves" in the most uses sections of road. Asphalt is a matrix based material, with the gravel being supported and held in place by the rubbery bitumen. This allows for the road to move and flex without breaking with heavy loads. I don't really see that property in a rigid, extruded plastic material, at least not the the extent of asphalt.
